coredata.dc:description: Urea-formaldehyde resins (UF) are the most commonly used wood-based panels adhesive in industry. These adhesives are more than 80 % by volume of the wood adhesives market. However, due to formaldehyde toxicicity and extreme volatility UF resins yield panels with formaldehyde emission problem both during wood panels preparation and their in-service use. In order to address this problem, to find an environment friendly replacement for formaldehyde to manufacture novel and safe aminoresins is essential research for wood adhesives. In this article, a bio-based amino resin wood adhesive (OGU) is developed by using oxidized glucose reacted with urea. The research work presented here tests the impact on the adhesive properties of a number of oxidation treatment parameters and of the glucose to urea molar ratio. The molecular structure and thermal properties of the OGU adhesive were studied by different analytical techniques. The results indicate that the bioaldehydes are obtained by glucose under mild oxidation conditions. The bioaldehydes obtained can then be reacted with urea to form a novel oxidized glucose-urea amino resin, suitable to manufacture plywood. Under the specified process conditions at pH 4 and at a urea-to-glucose molar ratio of 1, the OGU adhesive yielded plywood with a dry strength of 0.99 MPa, 24 h cold water soaking wet strength of 0.77 MPa, and 3 h hot water (63°C) soaking wet strength of 0.76 MPa. These results satisfy the requirements of the GB/T 9846–2015 standard. The OGU resin adhesive prepared has then a good market potential to replace the current UF resins used in the industrial production of wood-based panels and as a novel biomass amino resin adhesive.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Urea-formaldehyde resins (UF) are the most commonly used wood-based panels adhesive in industry. These adhesives are more than 80 % by volume of the wood adhesives market. However, due to formaldehyde toxicicity and extreme volatility UF resins yield panels with formaldehyde emission problem both during wood panels preparation and their in-service use. In order to address this problem, to find an environment friendly replacement for formaldehyde to manufacture novel and safe aminoresins is essential research for wood adhesives. The research work presented here tests the impact on the adhesive properties of a number of oxidation treatment parameters and of the glucose to urea molar ratio. The molecular structure and thermal properties of the OGU adhesive were studied by different analytical techniques. The results indicate that the bioaldehydes are obtained by glucose under mild oxidation conditions. The bioaldehydes obtained can then be reacted with urea to form a novel oxidized glucose-urea amino resin, suitable to manufacture plywood. Under the specified process conditions at pH 4 and at a urea-to-glucose molar ratio of 1, the OGU adhesive yielded plywood with a dry strength of 0.99 MPa, 24 h cold water soaking wet strength of 0.77 MPa, and 3 h hot water (63°C) soaking wet strength of 0.76 MPa. These results satisfy the requirements of the GB/T 9846–2015 standard. The OGU resin adhesive prepared has then a good market potential to replace the current UF resins used in the industrial production of wood-based panels and as a novel biomass amino resin adhesive.

ce:section.ce:para: Urea-formaldehyde resins (UF) have the advantages of low cost, simple preparation, ease of use, low curing temperature, fast curing rate, light color of the cured resin, and of good bonding properties. It is for this reasons that they have been and are widely used in the production of indoor plywood, particleboard, fiberboard, and other wood composites. UF resins are then the dominant adhesive in the wood industry (Pizzi,1994, Despres et al., 2010). However, the presence of formaldehyde emissions in UF and its bonded products can be harmful to the environment and human health (Dazmiri et al., 2019). Many researchers have carried out considerable work in reducing the amount of formaldehyde released by UF resins (Raydan et al.,2021, Bono et al., 2003, Tohmura et al., 2001, Lu et al., 2021, Mansouri and Pizzi, 2006). Reducing the amount of formaldehyde used has been one of the effective ways used to reduce formaldehyde release by UF resins, but it does also tend to significantly reduce the bonding effectiveness of UF resins.

To completely solve the UFs problem of formaldehyde emission, some other aldehydes such as propionaldehyde (Mansouri and Pizzi, 2006), Succinic aldehyde (Mamiński et al., 2008), glutaraldehyde (Maminski et al., 2011) and dimethoxy acetaldehyde (Despres et al., 2008, Deng et al., 2014) were used to replace formaldehyde to react with urea to prepare new amino resins wood adhesives. In comparison to the UF resin adhesives, plywood made using these new amino resins adhesives has a clear formaldehyde emission-free advantage. However, the aldehydes used in these studies are petrochemicals-derived but still of various levels of toxicity, environmentally harmful, and non-renewable. Therefore, to develop biosourced aldehydes readily available and with excellent environmental property as an alternative to formaldehyde to prepare amino resins wood adhesives is still significant and meaningful research work.

More recently, some interesting research works have reported the formation of bioaldehydes by specific oxidative treatments of carbohydrates and then used them as a crosslinking and curing agent for wood adhesives (Xi et al., 2022, Frihart and Lorenz, 2019, Song et al., 2023, Fan et al., 2020, Xi et al., 2020). Among these methods, Frihart utilized oxidants like periodate and permanganate to convert carbohydrate components in plant protein flours into aldehydes. These aldehydes can subsequently react with the amino groups present in the protein chain, resulting in the formation of a robust hardened network. This process enhances both the gluing strength and the water resistance of soybean flour adhesive (Frihart and Lorenz, 2019). Inspired by this finding, our research group created a resin with a network structure that is obtained by oxidizing sucrose with various oxidizing agents and then reacted with hexamethylenediamine under mild conditions by a Schiff base addition action, which assured a igh adhesive qualities (Song et al., 2023). However, since this reaction was carried out under milder conditions, a problem subsisted of some residual hexamethylenediamine. This implies the volatilization of the toxic hexamethylenediamine during the wood panels hot pressing, thus a detrimental occurrence for the environment and human health. Thus, hexamethylenediamine, a petrochemical-sourced product, is not sustainable, and its use is out of line with current environmental concerns.

As an organic chemical, urea contains two amide groups, which can react with aldehydes to obtain polycondensation resins. Urea is itself osourced, hence its use to synthesize bio-based amino resin adhesives by reacting it with biosourced aldehydes formed from carbohydrates specific oxidation will be of interest for wood adhesives. Hence, this research aimed to oxidize glucose using oxidizing agents to generated non-toxic and non-volatile bio-sourced aldehydes. These were subsequently reacted with urea to synthesize a novel bio-based adhesive called OGU resin. The purpose of OGU resin is to serve as an alternative to widely utilized UF resin adhesives for the wood industry. Furthermore, not only the reaction of oxidized glucose with urea, but also the optimum synthesis process of this new biomass amino resin will investigated in this work.
Glucose and Urea, Analytical pure, Guangdong Guanghua Technology Co., LTD.; Sodium periodate, Analytically pure, Shanghai Maclin Biochemical Technology Co., LTD.;

At room temperature, 10 g distilled water, 20 g of glucose and 2 g sodium periodate were added to a three-port flask with a thermometer, condenser and agitator in sequence. Turn on the switch and mix this solution for 45 min, then adjusted pH value with 30 % hydrochloric acid to 2, 4, 6 and added the planned mass of urea immediately. Increasing the temperature to 90 °C, keep this reaction for 110 min to obtain adhesives of OGU-pH2, OGU-pH4 and OGU-pH6. After the optimal PH value is determined, the molar ratio of glucose to urea is explored and prepared OGU-1:0.5, OGU-1:1, OGU-1:1.5 and OGU-1: 2 adhesives, their solid content was 72 %, 74 %, 77 % and 78 %, and the viscosity was 258.7 mPa·s, 271.8 mPa·s, 245.7 mPa·s and 268.6 mPa·s, respectively.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation of three-layer plywood and bonding effectiveness test
ce:section.ce:para: Three-layer plywood were prepared from poplar veneer (size 400 mm× 400 mm×2 mm), and the spreading amount of OGU adhesive is 270 g/m2.
Hot pressing condition: 200℃ temperature, pressure of 1.0 MPa and the pressing time is 5 min.

The prepared plywood was stored in a temperature of (20 ± 2) °C and relative humidity of (65 ± 5) % for 24 hours. The specimens were cut into 100 mm×25 mm by using a high-precision table saw (Shanghai Festo Equipment Co., Ltd.) and tested according to GB/T 17657–2022. Each test is repeated 7 times.

The tests were conducted using an iS50 infrared spectrometer (Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrometer, Nicolet, USA) with a range of 500 and 4000 cm−1 and to scan the KBr compression sheet 32 times at the resolution of 1 cm−1.

XPS analyse was conducted using a Thermos Scientific K-Alpha+ type XPS apparatus, and tests were performed using the powder compact method. The spectrometer utilized monochromatic aika radiation at 1486.6 eV. The "CAE" scan mode is set by the analyzer.

Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS, Shimadzu, Japan) combined with electrospray ionization (ESI) was used in this research. The samples were tested under parametric conditions of 135 V, nitrogen as drying gas, flow rate of 8.0 L per minute, test temperature of 350 °C, and nebulizing (30 psi) gas.
The samples were tested using a DSC204 (Netzsch, Germany) with a protective gas of nitrogen, a heating rate of 10 K per minute, and a temperature increase from 30 °C to 250 °C.

The experimental work was carried out on the NETZSCH DMA-242 equipment. 0.125 g adhesive was evenly spread on the surface of two poplar wood plies (50 mm×10 mm×3 mm). And then three point bending mode was used in the test. The temperature increase range of 30℃-250℃, frequency of 10 Hz, dynamic force of 2 N, temperature increase rate of 5 K/min.

The thermal stability of the adhesives was tested using a NETZSCH STA2500 machine. For the test, 5–8 mg of dry powder was placed in a platinum disk. The sample was then heated 30 °C- 800 °C under nitrogen at a rate of 10 °C per minute.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Adhesive molecular structure and synthetic reaction mechanism analysis
ce:section.ce:para: The FT-IR spectra of urea, glucose, oxidized glucose and oxidized glucose-urea resin adhesives are shown in Fig. 1. By comparing the two infrared spectra of glucose (G) and oxidized glucose (OG), the 1721 cm−1 peak is assigned to the CO group stretching vibration inferring that glucose generates bio-aldehyde groups by oxidation sodium periodate oxidation (Zhang et al., 2023; Xu et al., (2022)）. Compared with urea (U), OGU does not exhibit v ariable angular vibration of primary amine NH2 at 1600 cm−1, but in the 3448 cm−1 to 3344 cm−1 range, the bimodal stretching strength of primary amine (NH2) of OGU is weak. This can be due to oxidized glucose reacting with urea amide groups, affecting the vibration of the -NH2 group (Mohsin et al., 2018). Moreover, the vibration intensity and peak width of the carbohydrates O-H tensile vibration at 3448 cm−1 ∼ 3344 cm−1 are smaller than in OGU. This may be due to OGU containing both -OH and -NH2, and hence their characteristic peaks are superimposed form a wider peak (Zhang et al., 2022)

To verify what occurs in the reaction of oxidized glucose with urea, XPS analysis was carried out to analyze the oxidized glucose and the oxidized glucose - urea resin. According to the literature, urea (U) exhibits two peaks of different carbon types, with the most common one found in the form of an amide-linked carbon (N-CO-N, 289.0 eV) (Biniak et al., 1997, Watts and Wolstenholme, 2019). The XPS full spectrum of OG and OGU ( Fig. 2a) shows that OGU is mainly composed of C, N and O elements. OG, however, consists mainly of two elements: C and O. In addition to the hydroxyl carbon (C-OH, 286.7 eV), methylene carbon/methylene carbon (C-C, 284.7 eV) and amide carbon (N-CO-N, 289.0 eV), a carbon with a binding energy of 286.3 eV was also detected in the OGU C1s spectra. This carbon is probably the product of the addition reaction of oxidized glucose and urea. Further analysis shows that the binding energy of aldehyde carbon changes from 288.4 eV to 286.3 eV, indicating that the chemical environment of such a carbon has changed. Therefore, it appears that the urea-aldehyde by addition of amino groups and oxidation of glucose does indeed form the structure of C-N.

In the XPS O 1 s spectrum (Fig. 2c), OG exhibits two peaks corresponding to different oxygen forms: Hydroxy-oxygen (C-OH, 531.9 eV) and aldoxy (CO, 531.3 eV) (Fan et al., 2017). By comparing OG O1s (Fig. 2c), the hydroxy-oxygen content in OGU remains unchanged, while the aldehyde oxygen content significantly decreases. This decrease can indicate that the CO group in the oxidation of glucose reacts with urea to form new substances, hence the relative content of aldehyde oxygen is significantly reduced (Kundu et al., 2008). This indicates that the aldehyde group in oxidized glucose reacts with the amide group in urea to produce a new substance containing a C-N structure.

In the XPS N 1 s spectrum (Fig. 2d), the nitrogen in OGU mainly exists in the form of amide nitrogen (N-CO-N, 398.7 eV). This is also detected in combination with 397.4 eV for nitrogen, this probably been due to the addition reaction of the oxidized glucose aldehyde group and the urea amide group, resulting in a new compound presenting a C-N structure (Lee, 2013). This result is in line with previous results in the XPS C1s spectrum (Fig. 2b). By observing OGU NIs (Fig. 2d), the binding energy of the nitrogen structure (397.4 eV) is smaller than that of urea nitrogen (398.7 eV). This study result is in line with the results of Dong et al. (Dong et al., 2019) and Steffan et al. (Steffan et al., 2008). Therefore, as a consequence of the above results, the reaction of the aldehyde generated by oxidation of glucose with the amide group can be analyzed, as well as to state that the reaction has yielded another product with a C - N structure (see Fig. 4).

To study the distribution of the OGU resin and the reaction mechanism of oxidized glucose and urea, the OGU resin was characterized by LC-MS ( Fig. 3). Based on the peaks in the spectrum, the possible structure of the polymer is shown in the Fig. 3. The 176 Da and 282 Da compounds consist of one OG molecule and one urea molecule. Similarly, 204 Da, 416 Da, and 443 Da are compounds with distinct branching structures. It can be inferred that when oxidized glucose reacts with urea, the aldehyde group in the oxidized glucose structure undergoes addition reaction with the amine group in the urea structure to form a substance containing C-N structures. From the above analysis, it can be seen that when glucose is oxidized to form biosourced aldehydes under the action of sodium periodate, at a certain temperature (90℃), the addition reaction between the aldehyde and the urea amide group can form a new compound also presenting a C-N structure. The reaction mechanism is shown in Fig. 4.

Fig. 5a shows the strength results of plywood bonded with the OGU resins at pH 2, 4, and 6, dry, after 24 h cold water soaking tested wet, and after 3 h hot water (63°C) soaking tested wet. At pH 4 the dry strength of plywood is 0.99 MPa, the strength of after cold water soaking is 0.77 MPa, and the strength after 3 h in hot water (63°C) is 0.76 MPa. These results meet China national standard (GB/T 9846–2015) requirements for second-class board, which stipulates a minimum strength of 0.7 MPa. However, at pH 2 and 6, the plywood strength results fall short of meeting the requirements specified in the standard (GB/T 9846–2015) for type II boards (strength ≥ 0.7 MPa) in terms of cold water and warm water strength. Conversely, conventional UF resins synthesized under acidic conditions have less desirable mechanical properties, even though formaldehyde release is low (Hse et al., 1994). Therefore, the performance of the OGU resin is better than traditional UF resins, and without any formaldehyde release.

Fig. 5b shows the bonding properties of oxidized glucose - urea resin adhesives prepared at different urea additions at pH 4. The first result to be noted is that the mechanical properties of plywood pressed directly with oxidized glucose without the addition of urea is 0. This is acceptable because oxidized glucose only forms low molecular weight compounds that cannot function as adhesives. As urea is applied to form the OGU resin the bonding markedly changes. In the molar ratio range 0.5–1.5 of urea to glucose the synthesized OGU resins show good adhesion performance. Especially when the ratio is 1, the OGU resin adhesive presents its best performance, with dry shear strength being 0.99 MPa, 24 hours of cold water soak shear strength 0.77 MPa, and 3 hours hot water (63℃) shear strength 0.76 MPa. These values satisfy the requirements of the Class II plywood national standards (≥0.7 MPa). Moreover, the properties of the plywood are comparable to those obtained with urea-formaldehyde resins (Weng et al., 2023). However, excessive urea will result in a poorer performance of this adhesive, such as the OGU-1:2. This latter has neither cold-water strength nor hot water, this being caused by the excess of urea left in the hardened adhesive which does easily dissolve in water thus damaging the glue layer.

The curing temperature peak observed in the DSC results can be used as an indicator of the curing reactivity of the tested adhesives (Li et al., 2013). Fig. 6a shows the DSC traces of the OGU resin at different pHs. As seen in Fig. 6a, the curing temperatures of the OGU-pH2, OGU-pH4 and OGU-pH6 resins are respectively 145°C, 120°Cand 160°C. Such a large curing temperature peak indicates the difference in curing reaction rates of the different OGU resins, and has clearly a direct correlation with the pH used. This also indicates that when the pH is 4, the OGU resin has the highest reactivity, explaining why the plywood prepared with OGU-pH4 shows the best bonding strength. Fig. 6b shows the effect of urea additions on the curing properties of the OGU resins, which were also tested by DSC. It's clear that resin OGU-1:1, has a curing peak at a lower temperature than the other resins. Thus, under the same curing conditions, OGU-1:1 possesses enough reactivity to form the best hardened network structure, thus resulting in better curing and bonding performance.

The DMA test results of the OGU resins in this study are presented in Fig. 7,. First of all, as can be seen from the figure, at the beginning of the warming period, as the test temperature increases, the DMA curve of the adhesives show a decreases in modulus value. This is attributed to the adhesive melting/softening and flowing as the temperature increases to penetrate into the wood veneers. As the temperature continues gradually to increase, the OGU adhesive begins to be cured and the modulus value also increases. Second, the slope of the curve segment where the energy storage modulus sharply goes up to the maximum modulus can indicate the adhesive curing reaction rate, as it has been already reported (Pang et al., 2020, Kamoun et al., 1998). In Fig. 7a, the initial curing temperatures of the three resins showed little difference, this being in line with the DSC results. The curing rate of the three resins can be roughly judged by the slopes of the curves at the higher part stage of the graph traces, with the curing reaction rate υOGU-pH4 > υOGU-pH6 > υOGU-pH2 (Amirou et al., 2015). In Fig. 7b, when the mole ratio is 1:1 for oxidized glucose and urea, the curing reaction rate and storage modulus are at the highest, which is about 5300 MPa. This is consistent with the mechanical test results of OGU resin at pH 4, at m(U): m(G)=1 it shows the best performance, and it is also consistent with the DSC analysis results in Fig. 6(b). Finally, when the temperature increases to more than 200 ℃, the DMA curves modulus values of the adhesives in both Fig. 7(a) and (b) show a decreasing trend. This is due to both the contribution of the adhesive degradation from this high temperature, and simultaneously to the charring of the wood also due to the high temperature, all this leading to the beginning of the decline in mechanical strength of the bonded joint (Xu et al., 2022).

Fig. 8 shows three cured OGU resins thermal stability results. The OGU adhesive pyrolysis process can be divided into two stages. The mass segment loss interval of the first order is 30°C-150°C. This stage is primarily concerned with water evaporation to dry the sample and reduce its quality, as the solid samples prepared absorb moisture from the air before the test. While this water remaining in the OGU cured resin is low, the mass loss of all OGU resins in this stage is only about 5 % (Roumeli et al., 2012, Stradella and Argentero, 1993). The second stage is a rapid thermal decomposition of the OGU resin between 150°C and 550°C, with most of the weight loss (about 65 %) occurring in this stage. In this stage, the molecular chain of the resins are degraded and broken, and the cured network structures are degraded too. The results indicate that when pH = 4, m(U):m(G) = 1, cross-linking between OG and U is more effective, leading to an improved thermal stability of the OGU resins, this being consistent with the previous analysis. The temperature for maximum thermal mass loss rate of OGU resins is 210℃, this being consistent with the results of the DMA test in which the value of the storage modulus starts to reduce at about 210℃.

In this the work presented, a novel bio-based amino resin adhesive has been successfully prepared by oxidizing glucose with sodium periodate and then to react its oxidation products with urea. At the pH of 4, at the urea and glucose molar ratio of 1, a synthetic resin adhesive with strong bonding properties and water resistance was prepared. The strength of the plywood panels bonded with this new resin after a 24 hours cold water soaking and after 3 hours immersion in hot water (63℃) were 0.77 MPa and 0.76 MPa, respectively. Thus, they fulfill the requirements of the relevant standards (≥0.7 MPa). FT-IR, XPS and LC-MS analysis confirmed that biosourced aldehydes were formed when glucose was oxidized by sodium periodate. At the temperature of 90℃, the biosourced aldehydes generated from oxidized glucose react with the amide groups of urea to produce compounds comprising a C-N structure. The results of DSC, DMA and TG tests show that the mechanical properties of OGU are the best and up to the standard when pH=4 and molar ratio of glucose to urea is 1. Therefore, the OGU adhesive prepared by the oxidation treatment without use of any petroleum derived aldehydes, is a green and formaldehyde-free wood adhesive. Furthermore its preparation is simple and its bonding performance is good, thus it does possess a great potential for industrial application.
